paraphrase: Worship of Rāma in his yantra with the mantra; without yantra the deity is not pleased.
Bṛhaspati asks Yājñavalkya about Avimukta; there Rudra gives the dying the tāraka, the Rāma mantra.
Oṃ's parts: a is Lakṣmaṇa, u Śatrughna, m Bharata, the half-measure Rāma; Sītā is the primordial nature.

Nārada asks Vāsudeva about the ūrdhvapuṇḍra; gopīcandana clay from Dvārakā is applied with mantras; householders mark twelve places, students and forest-dwellers fewer; the ascetic marks head, forehead and heart; the paramahaṃsa one mark on the forehead.
One should meditate on the flame in the heart as Vāsudeva, the self of all.

In the beginning there was the unmanifest light; it became twofold, green (māyā) and red (puruṣa); from their union came the golden egg and Parameṣṭhin, who asked 'what is my family, what my task?'; a voice told him to know by austerity.
After a thousand years of discipline he sees the supreme anuṣṭubh verse, and then the Lord Nṛsiṃha; by the mantra he creates.
Bṛhaspati asks Yājñavalkya about Avimukta; there the tāraka — 'oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya' — is to be known.
Oṃ's subtle parts and the syllables are identified with Rāma, Sītā and Rāma's companions; knowing this one is freed.
'Kṛṣ' denotes existence and 'ṇa' bliss; their union is Kṛṣṇa, the supreme Brahman.
The sages ask Brahmā who is the supreme god, whom death fears; Brahmā: Kṛṣṇa (Govinda) is the supreme god; his meditation form and his mantra are given.
Devotion is worship of him: fixing the mind on him with no desire for this world or the next; this alone is freedom from action (naiṣkarmya).

paraphrase: The gopīs ask Durvāsas; Kṛṣṇa is the Self, ever celibate though amid them; Mathurā is described as a maṇḍala; Kṛṣṇa is the one Lord in all.
The sages who wished to embrace Rāma in the forest are told they will be born as gopīs when he comes as Kṛṣṇa.

An allegory: Nanda is supreme bliss, Yaśodā liberation, Devakī Brahma-knowledge, Vasudeva the Veda, the gopīs and cows the ṛcs, the flute Rudra, Gokula Vaikuṇṭha, the trees ascetics, the demons vices, Balarāma Śeṣa, Kṛṣṇa Brahman, the 16,108 wives the ṛcs and Upaniṣads, Kaṃsa the Kali age.
Nārada asks Brahmā for the knowledge that gives liberation; Brahmā gives the Hayagrīva mantras with seers, metres and seed-syllables; one who knows them attains knowledge and liberation.
Brahmā asks Nārāyaṇa for the tāraka; Nārāyaṇa: 'I, Dattātreya, have been given (datta)'; meditating on Dattātreya one is freed.
His seed-syllable and mantras of various lengths are given with limbs and fruits.
The teaching passed from Brahmā to Nārada and others; Garuḍa's form with serpent ornaments, and mantras that remove the poison of snakes.
At the end of the Dvāpara age Nārada asks Brahmā how, wandering the earth, he may cross Kali; Brahmā: by merely uttering the name of the Lord, the primal Person Nārāyaṇa, one shakes off Kali.
The name is: 'hare rāma hare rāma rāma rāma hare hare, hare kṛṣṇa hare kṛṣṇa kṛṣṇa kṛṣṇa hare hare'.

paraphrase: These sixteen names destroy the evils of Kali; no better means is seen in all the Vedas; they destroy the covering of the jīva of sixteen parts, and then the supreme Brahman shines like the sun's rays when clouds disperse.

Asked the rule, Brahmā says there is no rule: whoever recites it, pure or impure, attains the same world, nearness, form and union; by three and a half crore repetitions one is freed of the gravest sins and even of the sin of abandoning all dharmas.
The body is made of the five elements, rests on six supports, has six flavours, seven constituents, three humours and two kinds of birth.

The embryo grows month by month: after one night a mixture, seven nights a bubble, a fortnight a lump, a month firm; head in the second month, feet in the third, and so on; in the ninth it is complete.
Excess of the father's seed gives a male, of the mother's a female, equal a eunuch; defects arise from the parents' state.

In the ninth month the embryo remembers its past births and vows: if freed from the womb it will resort to Sāṃkhya-yoga, to Maheśvara or Nārāyaṇa, and meditate on Brahman; touched at birth by the Vaiṣṇava wind, it forgets.
Counts of the body: 107 vital points, 180 joints, 109 sinews, 700 veins, 360 bones, and so on.
In the beginning there was neither being nor non-being; from the unborn arose darkness, elements, the egg and the Person with a thousand heads; from him all creatures.

He whose body is the earth, who moves within the earth and whom the earth does not know… whose body is the mind, the self… he is the inner self of all beings, free of evil, the divine, the one Nārāyaṇa.
The knower lives like a child, unattached, like one mute or mad.
This teaching is not to be given to one who is not calm, not a son or disciple.
The eight-footed haṃsa, the unborn she-goat of red, white and black, and the one Lord who is seen by some as the twenty-fifth, by others as the twenty-sixth principle.

Definitions: bondage is identifying self with non-self; liberation is its cessation; ignorance is that through which this happens; knowledge that which removes it; the states, sheaths, jīva, witness, kūṭastha, inner controller, pratyagātman, paramātman and māyā are each defined.

Questions are posed on Brahman, Īśvara, jīva, nature, the supreme self, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, the world, knowledge and ignorance, bondage and liberation, the teacher, the disciple, the learned, the deluded, the demonic, austerity, heaven and hell, the renouncer — and each is answered.
Caste belongs not to skin, blood, flesh or bone; the Self has no caste; caste is imagined for convention.

paraphrase: The renouncer is one who, having abandoned all dharmas and 'I' and 'mine', takes refuge in Brahman, knowing 'I am Brahman', the supportless.

Vyāsa asks Śiva to teach Śuka at his initiation; Śiva teaches the four great sayings as a secret teaching with seer, metre, deity and limbs, and explains 'prajñānaṃ brahma', 'ahaṃ brahmāsmi', 'tat tvam asi' and 'ayam ātmā brahma'.
Of the four castes the brāhmaṇa is chief, say the Vedas and smṛtis; who then is a brāhmaṇa — the jīva, the body, birth, knowledge, action or the doer of dharma?
Not the jīva, which is the same in past and future bodies; not the body, which is the same in all castes, and at whose burning the sons would incur the sin of killing a brāhmaṇa.

Not birth: many great seers were born of other beings — Ṛṣyaśṛṅga of a deer, Kauśika of kuśa grass, Jāmbūka of a jackal, Vālmīki of an anthill, Vyāsa of a fisherman's daughter, Gautama from a hare's back, Vasiṣṭha of Urvaśī, Agastya from a pot.
Not knowledge, for many kṣatriyas and others are seers of the highest truth; not action, for all act from their karma; not doing dharma, for kṣatriyas and others give gold.

The brāhmaṇa is one who has directly realized, like a fruit in the hand, the non-dual Self — without caste, quality or action, being-knowledge-bliss — and lives fulfilled, free of desire and passion, endowed with calm and restraint, untouched by pride and ego; this is the intent of śruti, smṛti, purāṇa and itihāsa.
Oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya: one who knows the eight-syllable mantra goes to Vaikuṇṭha; the heart lotus, the Lord shining like lightning, devoted to brāhmaṇas.
'Prajñānaṃ brahma'; first-person verses: 'I am free of delusion, of ignorance; for me there is no waking, dream or sleep; I am the witness'.
The jīva is Śiva and Śiva is the jīva; the jīva is Śiva alone; bound by the husk it is paddy, without husk it is rice — so the bound one is jīva, freed from karma Sadāśiva.

paraphrase: Salutation to Śiva in the form of Viṣṇu and to Viṣṇu in the form of Śiva; Viṣṇu is the heart of Śiva and Śiva of Viṣṇu; as Viṣṇu is full of Śiva, so Śiva is full of Viṣṇu.
The body is the temple and the jīva is Śiva; worship with 'I am He' (as in Maitreya 2.1–3).
The Puruṣa-sūkta is explained: the Person's pervasion in space and time, his giving liberation, his fourfold form as Aniruddha and the vyūhas; Vāsudeva taught this to Indra.

Paiṅgala, after twelve years' service, asks Yājñavalkya; from the witness with māyā arise the avyakta (Īśvara), mahat (Hiraṇyagarbha) and ahaṃkāra (Virāṭ); by quintuplication the gross elements and the world.
The three bodies and the jīva's waking, dream and deep sleep; the jīva wanders like a caterpillar.
By hearing, reflecting on and contemplating the great sayings one realizes identity; the knower is liberated while living; at the body's fall, like ghee poured into ghee, he merges.

Nārāyaṇa alone existed — not Brahmā, not Īśāna, not waters, fire and moon, heaven and earth; from his meditation arose fourteen persons and a maiden; later from his forehead came the three-eyed trident-bearer, and his sweat became the waters in which the golden egg arose, from which came Brahmā.
Ṛbhu teaches seven stages of ignorance (seed-waking, waking, great waking, waking-dream, dream, dream-waking, deep sleep) and seven stages of knowledge.
'This one is our own, that one a stranger' is the reckoning of the small-minded; for those of noble conduct the whole earth is one family.

paraphrase: The body is compounded of earth, water, fire, air and space; the senses of knowledge and action, their objects; mind, intellect, ego and citta with their seats; the three guṇas and states.
The one imperishable syllable is praised as the lord of beings, Agni, the Kumāra, the sun in the sky, Viṣṇu, time, the Vedas and the supreme imperishable.

Nidāgha asks Ṛbhu how he attained the state; Ṛbhu tells of his worship of Annapūrṇā and her mantra, and of the five delusions (difference, doership, attachment, reality of the world, separateness) she removed.
The sun is the self of the moving and unmoving; from Āditya arise beings, sacrifice, rain and food; 'you alone are manifest Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra; you are the Ṛg, Yajus, Sāman and Atharvan'.
The eight-syllable mantra of the sun, beginning 'ghṛṇiḥ', is explained syllable by syllable; reciting it facing the sun frees from disease and sin and gives the fruit of a hundred sacrifices.
Sāṅkṛti goes to the sun's world and praises the Sun with the Cākṣuṣmatī-vidyā; one who knows it has no eye disease and none in his family is blind.
The Sun teaches the seven stages of yoga — from good desire to the fourth — and the jīvanmukta who, seeing all as Brahman, is free.
Within the cave of the body dwells the one unborn, whose body is earth… (as in the Subāla); he is Nārāyaṇa.
Verses on removing the superimposition of 'I' on body and mind, abandoning vāsanās, samādhi, and liberation while living and without body; many are shared with the Vivekacūḍāmaṇi.
Savitṛ and Sāvitrī are paired as fire and earth, water and Varuṇa, air and space, and so on; the Sāvitrī mantra; the balā and atibalā vidyās remove hunger and thirst.

Aṅgiras teaches that the self is threefold: the outer (the body of skin, flesh, bone), the inner (the subtle knower who perceives through the senses) and the supreme (the imperishable Brahman beyond all attributes).
This teaching frees from saṃsāra even without agnihotra, Sāṃkhya or yoga: the body itself is the sacrifice.
Before eating one sprinkles the food with mantras and offers five oblations to prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna and samāna; the parts of the body are the fire, the priests and the ritual implements.

The gods ask Brahmā how the dead receive the rice-balls; the departed, as haṃsa, dwells three days in water, three in fire, three in space and one in wind; the ten piṇḍas form the parts of the new body.
Gopī means protector, candana the cause of joy — the bliss of Brahman; the clay marks the devotee.
Oṃ, this all is the one syllable; Gaṇeśa, with and without qualities, is the supreme Brahman.
Each verse praises the mind — that which goes far while awake and asleep, the light of lights, by which the sacrifice is performed — and prays: 'may that mind of mine be of auspicious resolve'.
